guidance: Pick the basis first: the portions you want or the eggs you have. Weigh the flour the result gives and crack the whole eggs it counts. Eggs cannot be split, so the batch grows slightly when the count is rounded up; the page says by how much instead of shorting the dough.
method: Fresh egg pasta is a dough of flour and eggs, so a batch is fixed by one number: how much egg goes with each 100 g of flour. At the 50 % default a 50 g egg goes with 100 g of flour, the one-egg-to-100-grams starting point; 45 % gives a drier sheet and 60 % a richer, yolk-heavy one. Starting from servings, the requested dough is the serving count times the grams per serving, the egg share of that dough is the dough times the ratio over 100 plus the ratio, and the egg count is the egg weight divided by the weight of one egg, always rounded up because an egg cannot be split. The flour is then the eggs actually used times the egg weight times 100 divided by the ratio, so the ratio stays exact and the batch grows by less than one egg instead of coming out short. Starting from eggs, the same relation runs the other way: flour is eggs times egg weight times 100 over the ratio. Dough weight is flour plus egg, and portions are the dough divided by the grams per serving. One US large egg supplies 50 g of egg without its shell, which is the default weight per egg and can be changed for other sizes. Every quantity is a dough quantity: the page does not cover cooking, drying, rolling or storing, and it is not a food-safety statement.

sources.title: Pasta — pasta is an unleavened dough of wheat flour mixed with water or eggs, the two ingredients this page scales
